The University Hospital Essen offers first class medical services in the Ruhr metropolis. Every year, 225.000 patients are treated in 30 clinics, 27 institutes and specialized centers. The over 8.000 employees offer medical care with state-of-the-art diagnosis and therapies, which meet highest international standards. Patient care is connected with basic and translational research at an internationally competitive level.Hemoglobin is best known for its role in oxygen transport in red blood cells. Our preliminary findings indicate that it is also expressed by lung immune cells, where it may contribute to antiviral defense. These findings further suggest that the thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1)/CD47 signaling axis limits hemoglobin expression and its associated antiviral antivity.The project aims to uncover the molecular mechanisms underlying hemoglobin-mediated antiviral defense and determine how this response is regulated by TSP-1/CD47 signaling. Combining mechanistic studies with in vivo models, we will explore whether targeting this pathway can enhance antiviral immunity while avoiding excessive inflammation and lung tissue damage.At the Insitute of Medical Microbiology (working group of PD Dr. Torben Knuschke), we are therefore offering the following position, which is fully funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG) and will start on 1 January 2027Perform in vitro and in vivo experiments to characterize the intrinsic and extrinsic (paracrine) funtions of hemoglobin in lung immune and epithelial cellsApply molecular biology techniquesPlan, perform, and analyze therapeutic intervention studiesPresent research findings at national and international conferences and contribute to peer-reviewed publicationsAssist in supervising Bachelors/Masters studentsA completed Master´s degree (or equivalent) in Biology, Molecular Medicine, Immunology, Biochemistry, or a related fieldSolid background in cell culture and standard molecular biology techniquesExperience in laboratory animal science (FELASA B) is an advantageStrong interest in basic research in Virology/ImmunologyIndependent, structured, and team-oriented working-styleExcellent written and spoken English skills; German language skills are a plus but not requiredAn exciting, methodologically diverse PhD project in an internationally visible research fieldDedicated supervision of the doctoral project within a cooperative working group with regular seminarsState-of-the-art laboratory infrastructure at University Hospital EssenInterdisciplinary work with colleagues from other departmentsEnrollment into the Graduate School for Biomedical Sciences BIOME (https://www.uni-due.de/biome)Salary according to the German public sector pay scale (TV-L, E13, 65%), fixed-term for 3 yearsA collegial working environment that encourages independent scientific ideasFamily-friendly corporate culture

GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel is a foundation under public law jointly financed by the Federal Republic of Germany (90%) and the State of Schleswig-Holstein (10%). It is one of the internationally leading institutions in the field of marine research.Through our research and our commitment to the transfer of knowledge and technology, we contribute significantly to the preservation of the function and protection of the ocean for future generations.The Research Unit Magmatic and Hydrothermal Systems (MuHS) of the research division 4 - Dynamics of the Ocean Floor is offering a position preferably starting as soon as possible. The position offers the possibility to attain a doctoral degree in natural sciences.The position is within the framework of the project “Understanding Core-Mantle Interaction Through Global Mapping of Ultra-Low Velocity Zones in Mantle Convection Models”, which is part of the German Science Foundation's Priority Programm SPP 2404 DeepDyn (https://www.geo.lmu.de/deepdyn/en/) about reconstructing the deep dynamics of planet Earth over geologic time.Ultra-Low Velocity Zones (ULVZs) are thin patches at the base of Earth’s mantle-only tens of kilometres high yet 100 to 1000 km wide-where seismic shear waves exhibit extreme reductions of 20-30%. They are archives of Earth’s thermochemical evolution, potentially reflecting its early differentiation or interactions with the core, but also more recent mantle flow patterns. Yet these interpretations depend critically on ULVZ composition, which remains poorly constrained.The doctoral researcher will numerically model ULVZ evolution and properties in plate-guided global mantle convection simulations. They will develop a framework that quantitatively evaluates these simulations by inferring ULVZ properties from mineral physics and comparing them to seismic constraints, including ULVZ geometry, geographic location and distribution. They will synthesize these results to deliver the first global ULVZ map based on dynamic simulations and to discriminate among proposed ULVZ compositions. GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel is a foundation under public law jointly financed by the Federal Republic of Germany (90%) and the State of Schleswig-Holstein (10%). It is one of the internationally leading institutions in the field of marine research.Through our research and our commitment to the transfer of knowledge and technology, we contribute significantly to the preservation of the function and protection of the ocean for future generations.The research group Plankton Imaging Technology and Deep-Sea Zooplankton Ecology at GEOMAR (in cooperation with Kiel University’s Marine Data Science Group) is offering a position in the project “MegaRays - Deciphering Underwater Light Fields for 3D Plankton Characterization” starting at the earliest possible date.The position is offered for a duration of 3 years, with the possibility of extension. In the first year, the successful candidate will be employed by GEOMAR at 75%, supplemented by a 25% contract at Kiel University. Years two and three are fully funded at 100% (pay grade E13 according to the collective agreement for the public sector, TVöD, depending on experience).The position offers the opportunity to pursue a doctoral degree in natural or computer science as a member of the “Helmholtz School for Marine Data Science” (MarDATA). MarDATA’s interdisciplinary focus spans supercomputing, modeling, (bio)informatics, robotics, statistics, and big data methodologies. Doctoral researchers benefit from a structured training program that promotes cross-disciplinary collaboration and provides in-depth scientific insight as well as a systematic approach to marine data science. For more information, visit: https://www.mardata.de/. As part of the MarDATA doctoral network, the project “MegaRays - Deciphering Underwater Light Fields for 3D Plankton Characterization” aims at exploring the use of underwater light field cameras for observing and characterizing plankton organisms (zooplankton) in the ocean. Light field cameras deviate from off-the-shelf cameras in that all rays have to pass through an extra microlens array that changes their direction. Effectively, this means photographing the object from several slightly different perspectives, allowing focussing or 3D reasoning after image capture. The German Diabetes Center (DDZ), Leibniz Institute for Diabetes Research at the Heinrich Heine University (HHU) Düsseldorf is an interdisciplinary research institute that links basic and clinical sciences to improve prevention, diagnosis and therapy of Diabetes mellitus and its complications. The Junior Research Group Crosstalk (head: Dr. Melanie Mittenbühler) at the Institute for Clinical Biochemistry and Pathobiochemistry focuses on how inter-tissue communication impacts energy balance and metabolic health. We are seeking a talented and highly motivatedPostdoctoral Fellow (PhD/Dr. rer. nat., m/f/div., E13 TV-L 100%) to join our research group. Our group investigates how skeletal muscle acts as an endocrine organ and communicates with other tissues through secreted signaling molecules, particularly myokines. In the ERC Starting Grant project MYOSCAN, we systematically investigate how exercise and age-related muscle loss alter the skeletal muscle secretome. We aim to identify novel exercise-sensitive myokines and define their roles in sarcopenia, metabolic disease, and cancer biology. A central question is whether muscle-derived factors promote or suppress tumor growth and how these signaling pathways can be therapeutically targeted.PhD in molecular biology, cell biology, biochemistry, physiology, exercise science, metabolism, cancer biology, or a related fieldStrong expertise in at least one of the following areas: proteomics/mass spectrometry, secretome analysis, cell biology, molecular signaling, metabolic research, or cancer biology. Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) is one of the largest universities in Germany. Thanks to its location in the Rhine-Main science region, the university can unfold to its full potential and showcase its innovative power and dynamism. Its status as a comprehensive university allows for multidisciplinary learning and teaching and has great potential for internationally renowned, interdisciplinary research. Almost all of its institutes are located on a single campus close to the Mainz city center - creating a lively academic culture for researchers, teaching staff, and students from every continent.Academic staff member (Postdoc): Plant RNA BiologyThe Wachter group investigates the molecular mechanisms and biological functions of alternative RNA splicing in plants (https://mps-imp.biologie.uni-mainz.de/). Our recent work has identified novel components of the plant splicing-regulatory code, including structured mRNA elements (e.g., https://doi.org/10.1111/tpj.71060 ) and position-dependent functions of pyrimidine motifs (https://doi.org/10.1111/tpj.16739). By combining these functional studies with global profiling approaches, we are building a framework to understand and engineer alternative splicing in the context of plant development and stress responses.As a member of our international research team, you will examine the regulation and functional impact of splicing decisions controlled by polypyrimidine tract-binding proteins (PTBs), a family of key splicing regulators in plants and animals. Your work will build on our previous findings on PTB functions in alternative splicing and on recent results from ongoing transcriptome-wide approaches, including splicing pattern profiling, iCLIP, and TRIBE. You will further develop these analysis pipelines and integrate the resulting datasets to define the role of this central component of splicing control in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. The new insights from these mechanistic studies will be linked to physiological PTB functions we previously observed, including ABA-dependent seed germination and drought tolerance. The overarching goal of this project is to establish the molecular connections between PTB functions and key traits of stress physiology, thereby laying the groundwork for novel strategies to enhance plant resilience. Neuronal exocytosis is a highly regulated process that enables the rapid release of neurotransmitters from synaptic vesicles. Central to this process is the controlled assembly of SNARE protein complexes, which drive membrane fusion and are regulated by a network of associated proteins. The PhD project will investigate the structural and molecular mechanisms underlying SNARE complex assembly and function in membrane-like environments. A particular focus will be placed on the development and characterization of membrane-mimetic systems, including lipid nanodiscs and synthetic copolymers, to study SNARE complexes and their regulatory proteins under increasingly native-like conditions. Cryo-electron microscopy will be combined with complementary biochemical and biophysical approaches to characterize these systems at the molecular level.The project offers the opportunity to work in an interdisciplinary structural biology environment at Forschungszentrum Jülich, with access to expertise in cryo-EM, NMR spectroscopy and X-ray crystallography. Cryo-EM studies will be conducted at the state-of-the-art facilities of the Ernst Ruska-Centre (ER-C) at Forschungszentrum Jülich. The expertise in NMR spectroscopy and macromolecular crystallography at IBI-7 offers further opportunities for complementary structural and biophysical characterization. This combination of methods will enable the candidate to address biological questions from different structural perspectives and to develop a broad expertise in modern structural biology. The German Diabetes Center (DDZ) is the Leibniz Institute for Diabetes Research at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf. The DDZ has the aim to develop new approaches for prevention, early detection and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and to improve therapy and treatment of its complications.The Institute for Clinical Diabetology (Director: Prof. Dr. Michael Roden) is looking for anEpidemiologist (postdoc - m/f/d) We are searching for a candidate with (1) a doctoral degree in epidemiology, (bio)statistics or a comparable discipline, (2) the ability to work in an interdisciplinary manner with physicians and life scientists, and (3) knowledge of epidemiological methodology and statistical analysis systems (e.g. SAS or R).
